Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Jharkhand: temples, megaliths and rock art

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Jharkhand's heritage includes the terracotta temples of Maluti, Mughal Rajmahal, the Chero forts of Palamu, the Nagvanshi palace at Navratangarh, rock art at Isko, megaliths at Pankri Barwadih and Chokahatu, the multi-faith site of Itkhori and the Jain hill of Parasnath. It has no UNESCO World Heritage Site.

We design study tours to Jharkhand's rock art, megaliths and temples for groups on request.

Why Jharkhand's heritage matters

Jharkhand is the Chota Nagpur plateau, a land of forests, rivers and minerals, and home to Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho and many other Adivasi communities. Its heritage is less about large royal monuments and more about stone, earth and living tradition: rock shelters, megaliths raised by communities that still honour their dead, painted village walls and sacred groves. That makes it one of the best places in India to study how archaeology and anthropology meet; our tribes of India guide gives the background.

Kingdoms did rule here too. The Nagvanshi rulers of Chota Nagpur, the Chero kings of Palamu, Mughal governors at Rajmahal and later zamindars all left buildings.

Museums in Jharkhand

  • Jharkhand State Museum, Ranchi. Sculpture, archaeological finds and ethnographic collections.
  • Tribal Research Institute Museum, Ranchi. Objects and displays on Jharkhand's Adivasi communities.
  • Sanskriti Museum, Hazaribagh. Private museum on Hazaribagh's rock art and Sohrai and Khovar painting.

Rock art and megaliths in Jharkhand

Isko, in Hazaribagh district, has a rock shelter with paintings and engravings, including geometric patterns and animal forms, whose dates are uncertain. Researchers have pointed out similarities between these designs and the Sohrai and Khovar wall paintings that women in the region still make on mud houses at harvest and marriage, though a direct line is hard to prove. Our rock art of India session discusses these comparisons.

Megaliths are common. At Pankri Barwadih, near Barkagaon, two standing stones are aligned so that on the equinoxes the sun rises between them, according to observers. Chokahatu, near Ranchi, is a large Munda burial ground (sasandiri) with hundreds of flat stone slabs, still in use. Here the past is not separate from the present: these are community places, and visitors should ask permission. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how archaeologists approach such sites with respect.

Ancient temples in Jharkhand

Maluti, in Dumka district, has a remarkable cluster of small brick temples, built mostly from the 17th to 19th centuries under the local Baj Basanta rulers, with terracotta panels of scenes from the epics and daily life. Many are in poor condition, and conservation work has been undertaken. The style links closely to Bengal terracotta temples.

Deoghar's Baidyanath temple is a major Shiva pilgrimage centre with a large monsoon gathering. The Jagannath temple in Ranchi was built in 1691 by a Nagvanshi ruler. Parasnath hill (Shikharji), the highest point in the state, is one of the holiest Jain pilgrimage places, where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are believed to have attained liberation. Itkhori, in Chatra district, has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain remains together, including votive stupas and sculpture. Benisagar, in West Singhbhum, has excavated temple remains and a large tank. Our Reading sculpture session helps groups identify images at such sites.

Forts and later monuments

The two Palamu forts, in the Betla area, were strongholds of the Chero kings, built in stone on hills in the 17th century, and were attacked by Mughal forces. Navratangarh, near Gumla, is a 17th-century palace of the Nagvanshi rulers, with several storeys, temples and a stepwell; excavation has added to what is known of it.

Rajmahal, on the Ganga, was the capital of Bengal under Raja Man Singh, Akbar's general, in the late 16th century. The Jami Masjid, the Sangi Dalan and other ruins survive. McCluskieganj, founded in the 1930s as a settlement for the Anglo-Indian community, has old bungalows that tell a recent but distinct story.

Prehistory and early archaeology in Jharkhand

The Chota Nagpur plateau has a long Stone Age record. Palaeolithic tools have been found along rivers such as the Subarnarekha and Damodar, and microliths, the small stone blades of later hunter-gatherers, are common across the region. Our guide to the Stone Age in India explains these periods. Early copper objects and iron smelting sites point to a long history of metal working on the plateau, which fits with its rich ores.

Excavations in Jharkhand have been fewer than in neighbouring states, so many dates remain broad and new work regularly changes the picture. Sites such as Itkhori, Benisagar and Navratangarh have been studied by state and ASI teams in recent decades, and survey continues to record new rock shelters and megaliths. For students, Jharkhand is a good place to see archaeology as an active field, not a closed book.

This also means that care matters. Many sites are on community land or are still sacred, and some rock art is at risk from graffiti and quarrying. Visitors who photograph rather than touch, follow local guidance and report damage to the authorities help protect them.

Living heritage: Sohrai, Khovar and festivals

Sohrai and Khovar painting from Hazaribagh received a Geographical Indication tag in 2020. Paitkar scroll painting, Dokra metal casting and bamboo crafts are other traditions. Festivals such as Sarhul, Karma and Sohrai mark the agricultural year. These are community events and should be visited, if at all, by invitation. Our lecture on culture and heritage looks at what it means to treat such traditions as heritage.

Planning a heritage trip in Jharkhand

Ranchi is the base for Chokahatu, the Jagannath temple and Navratangarh; Hazaribagh for Isko and Pankri Barwadih; Dumka for Maluti; Sahibganj for Rajmahal. Distances are moderate. Check the state archaeology department before you go, and ask locally before visiting megalith sites.

Questions people ask

What are the famous historical places in Jharkhand?

Maluti's terracotta temples, Rajmahal, the Palamu forts, Navratangarh, the Jagannath temple in Ranchi, Deoghar, Parasnath hill, Itkhori and the rock art and megaliths of Hazaribagh are the best known heritage sites.

Is there any UNESCO World Heritage Site in Jharkhand?

No. Jharkhand has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026. Its temples, forts and megaliths are protected by the ASI or the state, but none is on the World Heritage List.

What are the Maluti temples?

Maluti, in Dumka district, has a cluster of small brick temples built mostly between the 17th and 19th centuries, decorated with terracotta panels of epic scenes and daily life, in a style close to Bengal's terracotta temples.

Can we see megaliths in Jharkhand?

Yes. Pankri Barwadih near Hazaribagh and Chokahatu near Ranchi are the best known. Chokahatu is still a Munda burial ground, so visitors should go with local guidance and permission and behave as at any cemetery.
